title: The Firewall Problem That Turned Skyper Into Skype
dek: In 2003 a Swede, a Dane and four Estonians dropped their Wi-Fi plan, wrote their own internet-calling software and nearly ran out of money first.

story.founder: Niklas Zennström, Janus Friis, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu, Jaan Tallinn and Toivo Annus
story.event: Dropping a Wi-Fi sharing plan to write their own peer-to-peer calling software, and launching it short of money
story.summary: In late 2002 Niklas Zennström and Janus Friis began a project called Skyper with the Estonian programmers who had built Kazaa's back end; the plan was a Wi-Fi sharing network with internet calls as the attraction. Finding that existing calling software did not work behind firewalls, the team wrote its own peer-to-peer calling program and dropped the Wi-Fi idea. After a year in which Zennström said no venture capitalist would invest, Skype launched on 29 August 2003 and was downloaded about 10,000 times on its first day.
paragraphs: Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn had been writing software together since school; in 1989 they sold their first computer game to Sweden. Around 2000 they built the file-sharing engine behind Kazaa for two Scandinavians, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, much of it in Tallinn's flat in the Mustamäe district, where he worked from home as a young father. Kazaa brought its owners American lawsuits. In late 2002, inside Zennström and Friis's company Joltid, the group began something new. It was called Skyper, from "sky peer", and the plan was a network for sharing home Wi-Fi.

Internet calls were meant to be the attraction. Tallinn later explained that the team expected to run existing calling software on top of the network. Having tested what was available, he said, "none of them worked properly behind firewalls." The newest standard, SIP, needed a provider to set each user up, as email does, which for a network starting from nothing was a chicken-and-egg problem. So they chose to write their own peer-to-peer calling program, which people could start without anyone's help, and in time dropped the Wi-Fi idea altogether. Another account credits the voice idea to Friis and Toivo Annus, who managed the Estonian developers.

The building was slow and short of money. An early version went to about 20 testers in spring 2003, and the sound was glitchy. Because Skyper.com was taken, the r was dropped, and skype.com was registered that April. Zennström later said raising money took a year: the founders asked 26 venture capitalists for 1.5 million euros, for a third of the company, "But no one wanted to invest." His wife's salary kept them going. By one detailed account, development stalled that summer because developers could not be paid. The money that did come was led by Howard Hartenbaum, sent by the American investor William Draper, who wanted to back this team whatever it built.

Skype went live on 29 August 2003. About 10,000 people downloaded it on the first day; a German news agency put the first week at 60,000, and accounts agree on a million users within months. Two years after launch, Tallinn said, the founders sold their shares to eBay.

quote.text: If a man find a prudent companion who walks with him, is wise, and lives soberly, he may walk with him, overcoming all dangers, happy, but considerate.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The Wi-Fi plan was abandoned and the borrowed software proved useless, but the companions stayed the same. The verse puts the fellow-traveller before the route, and Hartenbaum, backing the team rather than any product, made the same bet.

reflection: Very little of what this group set out to build in 2002 survived. The Wi-Fi network went, the plan to borrow calling software went, and for one summer even the pay went. What carried through was a group that had already come through Kazaa's lawsuits together and knew how each of them worked.

When a plan you care about starts to fail, it can feel as if everything is failing. Often it is only the plan. The colleague who tells you plainly what does not work, or the person at home who carries more for a while, belongs to something slower and steadier, and is worth noticing before you need them.
invitation: Think of one person whose judgement you would still want beside you if your current plan had to change. Send them a short note today saying what you value in working with them, asking for nothing.

cross_checks.claim: Skype began in late 2002 as Skyper, a Wi-Fi sharing project, and the team switched to writing its own peer-to-peer calling software
Existing internet-calling software (SIP) could not do what the team needed, so Skype used its own technology
The name came from 'sky peer'; Skyper was shortened to Skype because the domain was taken
Raising money for Skype was hard: Zennström said it took a year
About 10,000 people downloaded Skype on its first day, and it had a million users within months

research_notes: Origin of the idea: Jaan Tallinn (Edge, 2015) says Skype started in late 2002 as a Wi-Fi sharing project and the team turned to its own VoIP after finding existing software failed behind firewalls; Ars Technica (Tänavsuu, 2013) agrees on the Wi-Fi plan but dates the germ of the idea to summer 2002 and credits Annus and Friis with the 'eureka' of peer-to-peer voice calls; the dpa report in Computerwoche (2013) says Zennström and Friis met in a Copenhagen park in summer 2002 to start an internet-telephony project. The story follows Tallinn's first-hand account, says 'in late 2002' for the start, and notes the other credit. Download and user figures differ: 10,000 on the first day (Ars, Estonian World, Invest in Estonia); 60,000 in the first week (dpa, consistent with the first); a million users 'within a couple of months' (Ars), 'a few months later' (Estonian World), 'within months' (Invest in Estonia); a CTA Hall of Fame profile says 'within a month' and was not used, since it also misstates the eBay deal. The story says 'within months'. Funding: Zennström (Wired, 2010; dpa) says fundraising took a year and 26 venture capitalists turned him down; Ars says Howard Hartenbaum, for William Draper, and other early angels provided the first millions. These fit together (the institutional funds refused, Draper's emissary said yes) and both are told; Ars gives $18 million later from a VC consortium, not used. The claim that development stalled in summer 2003 because developers could not be paid rests on Ars alone and is attributed as 'one detailed account'; Zennström's own remark that his wife's salary supported the family is consistent with it. The eBay price is not given in the story because sources differ: $2.6 billion (CS Monitor 2011, BBC 2005, Invest in Estonia), $2.5 billion (Estonian World), $3.1 billion nominal including earn-outs (Wired, dpa). Founder count: Tallinn and Ars both say seven people held founding shares (Ars names the seventh as Geoffrey Prentice); the story names the six usually called founders. The Ars article's later pages (/2/ and onwards) now redirect to the single-page version cited here. Kasesalu's and Heinla's roles are not separated in the story; dpa says Heinla did most of the programming.
